market_context: United States/general English; raw trimmed beef cuts compared per 100 g
title: The leanest cuts of beef

seo.title: Leanest beef cuts: fat, calories and protein per 100 g
seo.meta_description: Trimmed top round, eye of round and top sirloin references provide roughly 2.5–5.5 g fat per 100 g raw. Trim level matters as much as the cut name.
seo.search_intent: Identify low-fat beef cuts and compare them under matched raw, trimmed conditions.

excerpt: In trimmed raw USDA references, select top round roast is about 2.5 g fat/100 g, top round steak about 2.9–3.3 g, eye of round about 3.5 g and lean top sirloin about 3.5–5.4 g depending on the specific cut and grade. Visible fat can change the result dramatically.
content_html:
In beef, “lean” reflects both the muscle and how much external fat is left on it. For a fair comparison, these values use raw trimmed cuts per 100 g.

Cuts at the lean end

Raw USDA referenceCaloriesProteinFat
Top round roast, lean only, select~116~23.6 g~2.5 g
Top round steak, lean only~121~23.6 g~2.9 g
Eye of round, trimmed to 0 in fat~124~23.3 g~3.5 g
Top sirloin, lean only, select~127~22.3 g~3.5 g
Top sirloin cap, lean only~134~21.4 g~5.4 g

Trimming changes the number

A lean-only top-round reference can contain about 3 g fat/100 g, while a reference from the same general area with separable fat included can exceed 7–8 g. The label “top round” alone is not enough.

Cooking concentrates nutrients per 100 g

Raw values keep the comparison matched. As water is lost during cooking, cooked beef commonly contains more protein and fat per 100 g than the raw starting cut.

Lean beef still supplies iron and zinc

A raw lean top-round reference around 2.9 g fat provides about 2.3 mg iron/100 g. Trimming fat does not remove the characteristic mineral contribution of beef.

Choosing a lean beef cut starts with understanding that the name of the cut is only part of the answer. The amount of visible and internal fat varies with trimming, grade, animal and preparation. Cuts from the round and loin often have lean options, while ribs and heavily marbled steaks are usually higher in fat. In the United States, labels such as 'lean' and 'extra lean' have regulatory definitions based on fat and saturated fat per serving, so a package carrying those claims gives more specific information than a broad rule about which anatomical section is best.

Trimming changes the final plate. A steak with a thick external fat cap can be cooked with or without it, but eating the cap adds substantially more fat than trimming it away. Ground beef is even more straightforward because the percentage lean is printed on the package: 90% lean and 80% lean are different products even though both are beef. Cooking method can remove some rendered fat, yet it cannot turn a heavily marbled cut into the nutritional equivalent of a genuinely lean one.

Lean does not mean dry if the cut is cooked appropriately. Eye of round, top round, sirloin tip and some loin cuts can become tough when overcooked because they contain less intramuscular fat to buffer moisture loss. Using a thermometer, slicing against the grain, marinating for flavor or choosing moist cooking for tougher cuts can improve the result without adding large amounts of saturated fat. Tenderness depends on connective tissue and muscle use as well as fat, so the leanest-looking steak is not always the easiest to cook quickly.

Nutrition also depends on portion and the rest of the meal. Lean beef can provide protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12, but a very large serving still contributes more calories and saturated fat than a moderate one. Pairing a lean portion with vegetables, beans or whole grains changes the overall pattern more than obsessing over a few grams between two similar cuts. If the goal is lower saturated fat, compare labels, choose visibly lean cuts, trim external fat and rotate beef with fish, poultry and plant proteins rather than relying on one 'perfect' steak.

Bottom line

Top round, eye of round and well-trimmed top sirloin are among the leanest widely available beef cuts. Check visible fat and trim level, not only the cut name.

Choosing a lean cut is only part of keeping beef relatively low in fat. Visible fat around the edge can be trimmed before or after cooking, and methods such as grilling, broiling, roasting, or pan-searing without heavy sauces make the final serving easier to assess. Ground beef needs separate attention because its fat percentage is stated on the package rather than visible as a fat cap. A lean cut can also become a much richer meal when it is paired with butter-heavy sauces, cheese, or large portions, so the cut, serving size, and preparation all shape the final nutrition profile.

faq.question: What beef cut has the least fat?
faq.answer: Very well-trimmed top-round references can be around 2.5–3 g fat per 100 g raw.

faq.question: Is tenderloin always the leanest?
faq.answer: No. Trimmed round cuts can contain less fat than some tenderloin or sirloin references.

faq.question: Does lean beef still contain iron?
faq.answer: Yes. A lean top-round reference provides about 2.3 mg iron per 100 g raw.
